newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin starts second weekend in hospital.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin starts second weekend in hospital.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin began a second weekend in hospital fighting pneumonia on Saturday but the Kremlin has said he is recovering steadily and should be able to leave in a few days' time.
But, continuing the cautious tone which has crept into recent official statements on Yeltsin's illness, his spokesman said he needed time to recover to avoid a dangerous relapse.
"The president is certainly interested in recovering as quickly as possible," Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing.
"But I think it is natural to...show some patience, to give him the chance of recovering completely. A relapse is very dangerous and God forbid that there should be such a relapse."
Yeltsin's political opponents have used the pneumonia, which follows six months out of the Kremlin last year with heart problems, to argue that he is not well enough to rule.
They point to an economic crisis which has left millions of Russians struggling without pay and pensions and say that his ill health has brought a damaging drift in policy on all fronts.

The Kremlin has fought back, saying Yeltsin has been working during his convalescence. He spent three hours working on letters, decrees and an annual state of the nation address to parliament on Friday, Yastrzhembsky said.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin addressed the second concern, which is shared by some diplomats and economists who fear that market reforms are slowing down.

"The West should not worry. Reforms are not stopping, it's just that we don't have much money. But the desire (to reform) is great," he told reporters. "There have been reforms and there will be reforms. There will be no U-turns in Russia," he said.
Opposition efforts to force Yeltsin out have been hamstrung by the constitution, which does not specify how a decision on a president's capacity to rule should be made or by whom.
It also concentrates huge powers in Yeltsin's hands in areas like foreign policy, where relations with NATO have entered a critical stage.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana is due in Moscow on Monday to try to soothe Moscow's anger over the alliance's plans to issue invitations to some former East Bloc countries in July.

Alliance sources said in Brussels on Friday that Solana would give Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov a revamped package of measures offering Russia an upgraded relationship with the alliance to ease its security fears over the expansion.

The centrepiece of the package is an offer of some kind of permanent consultative forum between NATO and Russia, which has mooted uniting with its western neighbour Belarus in response to NATO's enlargement plan.
Within Russia, tensions are building in the run-up to elections in Chechnya on January 27 which follow a 21-month conflict between Russian troops and Chechen rebels.

Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov said on Friday that the troops, the last of which were withdrawn earlier this month, should be sent back if any of the Russians still living in Chechnya come to any harm.
Some Russian politicians have also said the election, which may exclude refugees living outside the region and will almost certainly bring a dedicated separatist to power, will be unfair.

Yeltsin, who sparked the conflict by sending in troops and tanks in December 1994, has kept a low profile at sensitve moments of the Chechnya crisis and his spokesman said on Friday he was not aware of his view on the concerns.
